title: The Trouble With Leader Theory
author: Nick Hart
summary: Hart's contention is that the inherited canon of leadership theory was built for a world that no longer exists. Tracing the line from Great Man through traits, behaviours, situational models, transactional and distributed leadership to today's authentic and ethical variants, he notes that the language keeps changing while the assumptions do not: leadership remains something fixed, located in individuals and done to others. The central diagnostic error he identifies is treating the complex as merely complicated, as though a school were a machine where the right lever, the right initiative or the right CPD reliably improves performance, with a heroic leader diagnosing and prescribing. Complicated systems have stable, repeatable variables; schools do not, because cause and effect cannot be disentangled and solutions do not transplant across contexts or time. He illustrates this with the observation that each new academic year produces a different school, since both the incoming cohort and the returning staff have changed. The proposed shift moves from leader and leaders to leadership as something emerging through daily relational work. Hart then asks how we would know leadership had happened, rejecting inputs such as plans written and emails sent in favour of outputs: direction, alignment and commitment.
points: The complicated-versus-complex distinction is the hinge of the argument, because it explains why importing another school's successful strategy so often fails.
Hart's test for whether leadership has occurred is deliberately output-based: not the plan written or the training delivered, but whether direction, alignment and commitment are present in the group.
The line that you never step in the same school twice extends Heraclitus to staffing and cohort turnover, and makes the case that leadership conditions reset continuously rather than annually.
Because leadership is defined as emergent, Hart notes it can be initiated by someone with no formal role, or even by someone external to the team entirely.
Direction, alignment and commitment are each given a working definition, with alignment meaning the coordination of knowledge and work and commitment meaning mutual responsibility for shared goals.
quotes: But while the language has changed, the underlying assumptions often haven’t. Most of these theories still treat leadership as something fixed, something people do to others; located in individuals and the roles they occupy.

Apply the right initiative, add some CPD, and performance improves. And inevitably, the right initiative is conceived by a heroic leader who is the only one capable of diagnosing the problem and implementing a solution.

In complexity, disentangling cause and effect is impossible; there is no single dial to turn or lever to pull; and we can’t simply transplant our previously successful solutions to novel problems (or others’ solutions to our problems).

At the start of every academic year when welcome new cohorts and some new staff, we have a new school because the people have changed. Not just that though, the people that remain will have changed too, shaped by our past year, our team and our evolving understanding.
Leadership isn’t a job description or a directive, it’s born out of interactions between people in corridor conversations, in planning meetings, in the micro moments of trust and influence.
Direction is the shared purpose; alignment is the coordination of knowledge and work to pursue that purpose; commitment is the mutual taking of responsibility for achieving of shared goals.
